q: What is employment at will?
r: Either side may end the job at any time for any lawful reason
Illegal reasons such as discrimination are still prohibited.
w: Employees can only be fired after a written warning
Warnings are not required in at-will states.
Employers must give a reason and a year's notice
Employees must stay for a minimum of one year

q: What does the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) establish?
r: Minimum wage, overtime pay and child labor rules
It covers many private employers.
w: The FLSA is about wages and hours.

q: What is overtime pay?
r: Extra pay, usually 1.5 times the regular rate, for hours over 40 in a week
Many non-exempt workers qualify.
w: A bonus paid once a year

q: What is the difference between exempt and non-exempt employees?
r: Exempt employees are not entitled to overtime; non-exempt employees are
Salary and duties determine the category.
w: Exempt employees must work overtime for free; non-exempt may not
Exempt means not entitled to overtime pay.

q: A non-exempt worker earns $14 per hour and works 45 hours in a week. How much overtime pay is owed for the extra hours?
r: $105 for the 5 extra hours at $21 per hour
Overtime is 1.5 times $14.
w: $70 for the 5 extra hours at $14 per hour
$140 for the 5 extra hours at $28 per hour

q: What does the Equal Pay Act prohibit?
r: Paying men and women differently for substantially equal work
It is part of federal pay law.
w: Paying any worker above minimum wage
Paying workers on a weekly schedule

q: What does Title VII of the Civil Rights Act prohibit?
r: Employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin
It applies to most employers with 15 or more employees.
w: Age is covered by a different law.

q: What does the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) protect?
r: Workers age 40 and older
It bars age-based discrimination in hiring and firing.
w: It protects employed and applicant workers.
It applies to many private employers.

q: What does the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) require employers to provide?
r: Reasonable accommodations for qualified workers with disabilities
Unless it causes undue hardship.
w: A guaranteed promotion for disabled workers
Lower standards for all job tasks

q: Which is an example of a reasonable accommodation?
r: Providing a screen reader for an employee with low vision
It helps the employee do essential tasks.
w: Removing the employee's required job duties
Paying a bonus for the disability

q: What does the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) provide?
r: Up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for certain family and medical reasons
Covered employers and eligible employees only.
w: Unlimited paid leave for all workers

q: What is sexual harassment?
r: Unwelcome sexual conduct that creates a hostile or offensive work environment
It is a form of sex discrimination.
w: Friendly teamwork on a group project

q: What should an employee do first if they experience harassment at work?
r: Report it through the employer's complaint process
Documenting events helps too.
w: Ignore it and hope it stops

q: What is retaliation?
r: Punishing an employee for reporting wrongdoing or exercising legal rights
It is illegal under many employment laws.
w: Giving an employee a fair raise

q: What does OSHA do?
r: Sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards
Employers must provide a safe workplace.
w: That is the Department of Labor under the FLSA.

q: What does OSHA require employers to do?
r: Keep the workplace free from recognized hazards
Employers must train workers on safety.

q: What is workers' compensation?
r: Insurance that pays for medical care and lost wages after a work injury
It is generally no-fault.
w: It is not a retirement plan.

q: A warehouse worker slips on spilled oil and breaks an arm. Which system most likely pays for treatment and lost wages?
r: Workers' compensation
It covers job-related injuries regardless of fault.
w: This pays people who lose their job.

q: What is unemployment insurance?
r: Temporary income for workers who lose jobs through no fault of their own
It is funded by employer taxes.
w: Pay for workers who quit without notice
A bonus for finding a new job
A loan for starting a company

q: What does the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) protect?
r: Employees' rights to organize and bargain collectively
It covers most private sector workers.
w: The right to a four-day week
The right to own the company

q: What is a labor union?
r: An organization of workers that bargains with employers over pay and conditions
It negotiates on behalf of members.
w: A government agency that hires workers

q: What is collective bargaining?
r: Negotiation between employers and a union over terms of employment
The result is often a written agreement.
w: A customer haggling over a price
A vote for a new CEO

q: What is a strike?
r: A work stoppage by employees to press demands
It is a form of protected activity in many cases.

q: What is a lockout?
r: An employer preventing workers from working during a labor dispute
It is the employer's counterpart to a strike.
w: A day off for all staff

q: What is a right-to-work law?
r: A state law that bars requiring union membership or dues as a job condition
Workers cannot be forced to join a union.
w: A law guaranteeing every person a job
It does not guarantee a job.
A law requiring unions at every firm

q: What does the Immigration Reform and Control Act require employers to do?
r: Verify each new hire's identity and eligibility to work
Employers complete Form I-9.
w: Ask for tax returns of applicants

q: What is E-Verify?
r: An online system for checking work eligibility of new hires
Some employers must use it.
w: It is not a tax tool.
A background check on credit scores
A system that sets pay rates

q: What is an independent contractor?
r: A person who is self-employed and controls how the work is done
They are not employees for payroll purposes.
w: That is a type of employee.

q: Which factor most suggests a worker is an employee rather than an independent contractor?
r: The company controls when, where and how the work is done
Control is a key test.
w: The worker uses their own tools and sets their own hours
The worker serves many different clients
The worker sends invoices for each project

q: What is a non-compete agreement?
r: A contract limiting an employee's ability to work for competitors after leaving
Enforceability varies by state.

q: What is a non-disclosure agreement (NDA)?
r: A contract to keep certain information confidential
It protects trade secrets.
w: A contract to share all company data

q: What is a probationary period?
r: An initial time to evaluate a new employee's fit for the job
Terms are set by the employer.
w: A period when the employee pays the company
A period when the company cannot fire anyone
A guaranteed contract for five years

q: What is wrongful termination?
r: Firing an employee for an illegal reason
Examples include discrimination or retaliation.
w: Laying off workers due to budget cuts
Ending a probationary period for poor performance

q: An employee is fired a week after reporting a safety violation to OSHA. Which claim is most likely?
r: Retaliation
Firing for reporting is illegal retaliation.
w: This is a sales law concept.
This is a competition law issue.

q: What is a layoff?
r: A termination due to business conditions rather than employee misconduct
Employees may be rehired later.

q: What does the WARN Act generally require for large layoffs?
r: Advance notice, typically 60 days
Employers of 100 or more must notify.

q: What is a hostile work environment?
r: Workplace conduct so severe or pervasive that it interferes with work
It may result from discrimination or harassment.

q: Which is an example of lawful hiring practice?
r: Choosing the applicant with the best qualifications for the job
Job-related criteria are lawful.
w: Refusing to hire someone because of their religion
Asking applicants their age or plans to have children
Rejecting applicants based on their national origin

q: What is a bona fide occupational qualification (BFOQ)?
r: A job requirement based on a characteristic that is truly necessary
It is a narrow exception.
w: A preference for friends and family
A requirement any manager can invent
It is narrow and must be necessary.
A way to avoid all discrimination law

q: What is affirmative action in employment?
r: Efforts to increase opportunity for groups that were underrepresented or disadvantaged
Rules vary by context.
w: A ban on hiring from certain groups
A requirement to hire only relatives

q: What does the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) require before an employer uses a background check?
r: Written notice and the applicant's permission
Applicants must be told if the report affects the decision.
w: Nothing because background checks are always allowed freely
Paying the applicant for the report
A court order is not required.

q: What is a payroll deduction?
r: An amount withheld from an employee's pay for taxes or benefits
Both mandatory and voluntary deductions exist.
w: An extra bonus added to pay
A fine paid by the employer
It is not an employer fine.

q: Which is a mandatory payroll deduction?
r: Federal income tax withholding
It is required by law.

q: What is a minimum wage?
r: The lowest hourly pay an employer may legally offer a covered worker
States may set it higher than the federal rate.
w: It sets a floor, not a cap.
It applies to covered workers generally.

q: A state minimum wage is higher than the federal minimum. Which must a covered employer follow?
r: The higher state minimum wage
The most protective standard applies.
w: Employers must follow the higher rate.
The lower rate would underpay workers.

q: What is child labor law mainly designed to do?
r: Protect minors from unsafe work and keep them in school
It limits hours and hazardous jobs.
w: It does not set adult pay.

q: Under federal law, what are limits for 14- and 15-year-olds working during school weeks?
r: Limited hours outside school time and restrictions on hazardous jobs
They cannot work during school hours.

q: What is a worker's right under the Fair Labor Standards Act regarding breaks?
r: Federal law does not require meal or rest breaks, though some states do
State law may add requirements.
w: Federal law requires a one-hour lunch

q: What is a whistleblower protection law meant to do?
r: Shield employees who report illegal activity from retaliation
Several laws provide such protection.
w: It does not replace law enforcement.

q: What is vested in a retirement plan?
r: The employee's right to keep employer contributions after meeting service rules
Vesting schedules vary.
w: A fee charged by the plan

q: What law sets standards for private retirement and health plans?
r: ERISA
The Employee Retirement Income Security Act.
